title: Controlled Spillback: regional reserve quotas, staggered fail-open, and legal-boundary tagging
creator: Sofia Patel
description:
Background:
Redwood Dedicated customers require deterministic throughput guarantees while also enforcing data residency and legal-boundary constraints. Current fleet placement routes requests to the nearest available zonal pool; when capacity is exhausted we perform naive spillover to the next region which can violate residency constraints or produce costly cross-region egress.

Goal:
Design and implement a "controlled spillback" mechanism that: (1) reserves regional quotas to satisfy committed throughput, (2) provides staggered 'fail-open' policies for best-effort workloads, (3) tags requests and pools with legal-boundary metadata to prevent cross-jurisdiction routing where forbidden, and (4) integrates with autoscaling to avoid oscillation and ensure throughput SLAs.

Key constraints and non-goals:
- Must respect per-customer residency flags; if a customer disallows cross-border execution, do not route out of the permitted geofence.
- Avoid introducing centralized single points of failure or synchronous blocking calls on the request path.
- This work focuses on routing and reservation; it does not change the billing model or committed-contract accounting (handled by the billing team).

Design proposal (high level):
1) Regional Reserve Quotas: Maintain a lightweight quota ledger per dedicated contract keyed by (customer, region, model_variant) representing committed throughput (rps or tokens/minute). Quota checks happen in the router; when a request arrives we attempt to allocate from the local region quota first. If local quota is exhausted, attempt allocation from the same-region spare pool before considering cross-region candidates.

2) Staged Fail-Open Policy: Define 3 tiers for routing decisions for each route: HARD (never cross-boundary), SOFT (prefer same-region, allow cross-region if capacity shortage but mark request for auditing), and BEST-EFFORT (fail-open quickly to maintain latency). Each tier has configurable thresholds (e.g., <5% spare capacity triggers spillback).

3) Legal-Boundary Tagging: Enrich the request token with residency metadata at the ingestion boundary (account flags, contract constraints). All pools expose their 'jurisdiction' tags. The router enforces a simple ACL: request.jurisdictions_allowed ∩ pool.jurisdiction != ∅ to consider a pool.

4) Autoscale & Backoff integration: When cross-region spillover is active, we trigger a soft autoscale signal to the original region (prewarm policy) with dampening to prevent oscillation. Implement exponential backoff on repeated spillback attempts; if backoff persists, escalate to human ops and mark the customer's route for capacity review.

5) Circuit-breaker lanes: Introduce per-customer circuit-breaker counters to track the fraction of requests served outside the committed region in a rolling window. When the fraction exceeds a threshold, automatically transition the route to 'degraded' which enforces stricter routing or throttling.

Telemetry and SLOs:
- Metrics: regional_quota_allocated, regional_spillover_rate, cross_region_requests_by_customer, request_latency_by-routing-tier, circuit_breaker_trips.
- Alerting: spike in cross_region_requests or circuit_breaker_trips -> P0 pager.

Rollout plan:
Phase 1 (Design + simulation): implement reservation ledger simulator and run against 30-day trace from dedicated customers to validate thresholds (2 weeks).
Phase 2 (Router & flags): wire in router checks behind a feature flag, run controlled traffic tests with a single non-production customer and internal load (3 weeks).
Phase 3 (Autoscale integration): emit prewarm requests + dampening, run chaos tests (2 weeks).
Phase 4 (Gradual customer opt-in): enroll small set of production customers with explicit allowlist, monitor for 6 weeks, then enable wider rollout.

Trade-offs considered:
- Centralized ledger vs. distributed token-bucket: chose a hybrid ledger with per-region caches to reduce cross-region latency while keeping global correctness via periodic reconciliation.
- Strict enforcement vs. availability: providing staged fail-open modes enables availability for non-sensitive customers while guaranteeing hard-enforced residency for regulated customers.

Testing & validation:
- Integration tests exercising residency tags and ACLs.
- Load test scenarios that simulate region-wide preemption and ensure autoscale prewarm reduces spillovers over time.
- Security review focusing on residency metadata integrity and potential leakage in logs.

Operational runbook pointers:
- If circuit_breaker_trips, check region capacity util, restart prewarm controller, escalate to capacity planning.
- Dashboard: dedicated->Regional Rightsizing view (new), showing reserved vs used and spillover trends by customer.

Acceptance criteria:
- No cross-region routing for HARD-tier customers under normal operations.
- Spillover rate reduced by >=60% for enrolled customers after autoscale prewarm enabled in staged tests.
- Alerts fire correctly when circuit-breaker thresholds are exceeded.

2026-03-08 Security review kickoff (Marcus Chen): flagged log retention for residency tags; we will mask account identifiers in debug logs and add an allowlist for debug-mode exports.
